name: Threshold Cartography
description:
Released in 2201 on the one-year anniversary of the Shelf Compression Act — corporate legislation that rezoned twelve Tier 1 districts to make room for Tier 4 expansion — Threshold Cartography is a sprawling double album compiling twenty-three artists across the Shelf and Circuit underground. Organized by the anonymous collective known only as Groundworks, it was pressed onto bootleg data chips and distributed through mesh networks and dead drops in Circuit transit hubs. The album's structure mirrors a map of the demolished districts, each track named after a street or landmark that no longer exists.

The production ranges from raw Shelf noise to Circuit folk to fractured neural-ambient, unified by a bone-deep anger and a refusal to let demolished places be forgotten. Standout tracks include 'Olufemi Street (Before the Dozers)' by Thresh & The Undertow, a slow-burning dirge built on recycled demolition recordings and a single mbira loop; 'Compression Protocol' by an uncredited Shelf duo, two minutes of distorted vocals over industrial percussion that became a protest chant; and 'The Last Address,' a solo piece by Wren Abara-Lindqvist, recorded live in the rubble of the Olufemi-Strand community hall hours before it was cleared. Vantablack Media's legal division issued seventeen takedown orders. None of them worked.
creator: various (compiled by Groundworks Collective)
audience: Shelf residents, Circuit labor organizers, underground journalists, civil rights advocates
cultural_impact: Threshold Cartography became the defining cultural document of the Compression Act resistance movement. The chip was copied thousands of times over three years — its data degrading slightly with each generation of duplication, which fans came to regard as a kind of authenticity mark. Corporate security forces raided three suspected Groundworks safehouses in 2202. The collective was never identified. In 2204, a Tier 3 academic published a paper citing the album as primary historical evidence of the demolished districts' cultural life — the only surviving record of several of those communities. Vantablack Media's legal team attempted to have the paper suppressed. They failed.
story_hooks: A player character finds a fourth-generation chip copy of Threshold Cartography in the rubble of a Shelf building — the data is corrupted except for one track, which contains hidden steganographic coordinates leading to a Groundworks safehouse.
A Vantablack Media legal operative hires the party to identify and silence the last known member of Groundworks before the tenth anniversary of the Compression Act triggers a planned rerelease.
A Tier 3 archivist is killed shortly after publishing research citing the album — someone very powerful wants the demolished districts to stay forgotten.
